title: Beating the Scholar's Mate
setupTitle: Four moves that stop the mate

setup.label: Pawn to g6, blocking the queen
Knight to f6, once the queen has left h5
Then: knight to d4, or pawn to d5

beats.say: Queen to h5, bishop to c4, and mate on f7. It wins a lot of beginner games, which is why so many players keep trying it.
Against a player who knows the answers, it backfires. The queen comes out early, gets kicked around, and White falls behind in development.
We'll build the setup that stops the mate, then punish five ways White keeps trying. You're Black, so the board is turned around.
The ideas come from Yellow Rook's video on the Scholar's Mate, retold in our words and checked with Stockfish. Where the engine disagrees with the video, we say so.

beats.card: Four moves that stop the mate
beats.say: Four moves. Watch the list tick itself off.
White plays e4, and you answer with e5.
Queen to h5 on move two. It hits your e5 pawn, and it looks at f7.
Guard e5 with a move that develops: knight to c6. No need to rush.
Bishop to c4. Now two pieces aim at f7, and only your king guards it. That's the threat: queen takes f7.
The natural move is knight to f6, hitting the queen. It's the mistake the whole trick is waiting for.
Queen takes f7, checkmate. Your knight attacked the queen but did nothing for f7.
Instead, g6. It blocks the queen's road to f7 and kicks her at the same time.
The queen steps to f3 and lines up on f7 again. Same threat, new road.
Now knight to f6 is right: it stands in the queen's way, so f7 is safe. One move earlier, the same knight lost the game.
Stockfish already likes Black a little, about minus 0.3. White's queen has moved twice and nothing else is out.

chapters.title: White pushes g4
chapters.from: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6

beats.card: A pawn storm on move five
beats.say: The most common try now is g4. The plan is g5, to chase your knight off f6. If the knight leaves, f7 falls again.
Pawn to g4.
Bishop to g7 looks natural. Watch what g5 does to it.
Pawn to g5 hits the knight.
If the knight simply steps away...
...it's mate on f7 again. To be fair, Stockfish says bishop g7 still wins if you meet g5 with knight to d4. Playing knight to d4 at once is simpler.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6 g4
beats.say: Answer a wing attack in the centre. Knight to d4 hits the queen and eyes a fork on c2. Stockfish: about minus six.
The queen has to run, and d1 is the usual square.
Many players now play d6, opening the bishop toward g4. It still wins, but it's slow.
White gets time to kick your knight with c3.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6 g4 Nd4 Qd1
beats.say: d5 is the upgrade. It hits the bishop on c4 and opens your bishop toward g4, all in one move. White has to react now.

chapters.title: The d5 punch: two mates
chapters.from: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6 g4 Nd4 Qd1 d5

beats.say: White usually takes the pawn. Then your bishop comes out with a hit.
Pawn takes d5, and bishop takes g4, attacking the queen.
If White blocks with the knight...
...knight to f3 is check. The king's only square is f1.
Bishop to h3, mate. The knight covers g1 and h2, and the bishop gives the check.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6 g4 Nd4 Qd1 d5 exd5 Bxg4
beats.say: Pawn to f3 is more common. It attacks your bishop.
Knight to e4! It opens the road from your queen to h4. Whichever piece the pawn takes, the queen comes in. About minus eight.
Take the bishop, and it's queen to h4, check.
King to f1, queen to f2, mate. The knight on e4 guards f2. It's the Scholar's Mate, played against White.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6 g4 Nd4 Qd1 d5 exd5 Bxg4 f3 Ne4
beats.say: Take the knight instead, and the same check comes.
This time the bishop just takes the queen. Stockfish: about minus thirteen.

chapters.title: Against Ne2: the solid reply
chapters.from: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6

beats.say: Better players stop your knight jump before it happens.
Knight to e2 covers d4 and gets ready to castle. It's White's best move here.
Finish your development: bishop to g7. Keep the d-pawn at home, because it wants to go to d5 in one step.
White opens the other bishop, and you castle.
A common club move: pin the knight with bishop to g5.
Ask the question at once: h6.
If it takes, take back. You have the two bishops and nothing to fear. Stockfish: about minus 0.7.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6 Ne2 Bg7 d3 O-O Bg5 h6
beats.say: If it keeps the pin, g5 chases it again.
And now d5. White's king is still in the middle, so open the middle.
Three white pieces hit d5 and only two of yours guard it. It looks like you just lost a pawn.
Bishop to g4, an in-between move that hits the queen. Stockfish rates knight to b4 a bit higher, but this one is easier to remember.
No other square for the queen keeps things together, so it goes to e3.
Knight to d4, and the fork on c2 is back.
White trades, you take back with the pawn, and it hits the queen. White's best now is a quiet retreat to c1, still about minus two.
Greedy: queen takes d4, two pawns up. Then rook to e8, check, with the king still in the middle.
King to d2? Knight to e4 is check, and now your bishop on g7 hits the queen. It falls.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6 Ne2 Bg7 d3 O-O Bg5 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 d5 exd5 Bg4 Qe3 Nd4 Nxd4 exd4 Qxd4 Re8+
beats.say: King to f1? Bishop to e2, check.
King to g1, then knight to h5. Your bishop hits the queen and the knight hits the bishop. About minus seven.

chapters.title: Queen to b3: f7 again
chapters.from: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6

beats.say: Another try: the queen swings over to b3 and hits f7 a different way.
Queen to b3.
Queen to e7 guards f7, and Stockfish calls it about minus two for White. Good, but you can do much better.
Knight to d4 hits the queen and eyes c2. Yes, it lets the bishop take f7. About minus six.
Bishop takes f7, check, and your king steps up to e7. It looks wrong. Count White's problems: the queen, the c2 square and the loose bishop.
Queen to c4 is the only move that covers all three, for now.
So take that square away: b5.
Queen to c5, check, still guarding c2.
Your king takes the bishop.
And if the queen grabs e5, your knight forks king and rook. About minus nine.

chapters.title: White plays c3 first
chapters.from: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6

beats.say: The other way to cover d4 is a pawn: c3. It's weaker than knight to e2, about minus 0.8.
Pawn to c3. It takes d4 away from your knight.
Same plan as before: bishop out, then castle.
Same pin, same chase.
Same punch, same in-between move.
This time d4 is covered, so just take back on d5. You win the pawn back and gain time on the queen. About minus four and a half.
If the bishop takes, take with the queen. Two bishops, and White's attack is gone.
Some players hide the plan: bishop first, then queen to f3. From f3 the queen doesn't give you a free g6.
Queen to f3, aiming at f7.
Knight to f6 blocks the queen at once. Don't hurry your bishop to c5.
Against c3, play d5 anyway. The pawn looks loose.
Push e4. It hits the queen and cuts it off.
Queen to g3, and you take back in the centre. About minus 0.7.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Bc4 Nc6 Qf3 Nf6 c3 d5 exd5 e4
beats.say: Queen to e2 pins your e-pawn, so it can't take on d5.
Stockfish's choice is knight to a5, hitting the bishop. It's about level.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Bc4 Nc6 Qf3 Nf6 c3 d5 exd5 e4 Qe2
beats.say: The video likes knight to e5, threatening d3 check. It's a trap: against bishop to b5 check, White is fine.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Bc4 Nc6 Qf3 Nf6 c3 d5 exd5 e4 Qe2 Ne5
beats.say: But if the bishop drops back to b3, knight to d3 is check.
The king has to go to d1, and bishop to c5 hits f2 twice. About minus eight.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Bc4 Nc6 Qf3 Nf6
beats.say: Against d3, the d4 square is open: knight to d4.
The queen goes back, and you play d5 again.
Take back. Two knights in the centre, about level. Stockfish likes b5 here even more.
Some players go for the same mate twice: queen to h5, hitting d5.
Ignore it. Knight takes c2, check, forking king and rook. Your knight on d5 still blocks f7. About minus seven.

chapters.title: Your game plan
chapters.from: e4 e5 Qh5 Nc6 Bc4 g6 Qf3 Nf6

beats.say: The whole defence in three lines.
One. Count the attackers on f7 before every move. Knight to f6 only when it blocks the queen, never to hit her on h5.
Two. If White hasn't covered d4, put your knight there. It hits the queen and forks on c2.
Three. Play d5, not d6. It opens your bishop and gives White no time.
Most players who try this have one trick. Once it fails, they're behind in development, and you're the one attacking.
So play it against Stockfish next, as Black, from the queen's early sortie.
